'''Morrel H. Cohen''' (born 1927) is an American [[Theoretical physics|theoretical physicist]] of [[Condensed matter physics|condensed matter]]. He was a Professor of Physics at the [[University of Chicago]] from 1952 to 1981, and was appointed Louis Block Professor of Physics and Biology in 1972. He worked at the [[Exxon Research and Engineering Company]] from 1981 until 1996, and then served in an [[emeritus]] role there until 2000. He currently has post-retirement positions at [[Rutgers University]] and at the Chemistry and Chemical Biology Department of [[Princeton University]]. He has published over 280 peer reviewed documents and has over 24,000 citations, according to [[Scopus]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Scopus preview - Cohen, Morrel H. - Author details - Scopus |url=https://www.scopus.com/authid/detail.uri?authorId=7405993157 |access-date=2022-09-23 |website=www.scopus.com}}</ref>

== Biography ==
Morrel H. Cohen was born in the United States in 1927; his family resided in [[Massachusetts]]. Cohen received his high school diploma from the [[Boston Latin School]] in 1944. He received his B.S. from [[Worcester Polytechnic Institute]], [[Worcester, Massachusetts|Worcester]], Massachusetts in 1947; his M.A. from [[Dartmouth College]], [[Hanover, New Hampshire|Hanover]], New Hampshire, in 1948; and his Ph.D. in physics from the [[University of California, Berkeley]], in 1952. Cohen’s Ph.D. thesis advisor was [[Charles Kittel]]. Cohen thesis was "On Nuclear Electric [[Quadrupole]] Interactions in Crystals".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Cohen |first=Morrel H. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=E2xIAQAAMAAJ |title=On Nuclear Electric Quadrupole Interactions in Crystals |date=1952 |publisher=University of California, Berkeley |language=en}}</ref>

Cohen joined the University of Chicago as an instructor in 1952, achieved full Professor of Physics in 1960, and was appointed Louis Block Professor of Physics and Biology in 1972. In 1978, he was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]]. He continued at the university until 1981, when he took a position as Senior Scientist at Exxon Research and Engineering Company in New Jersey. During his time at Chicago, he consulted with industry, including with the [[General Electric Company]], [[Argonne National Laboratory]], [[Energy Conversion Devices]], [[Monsanto Company]], [[Union Carbide Company]], and [[Schlumberger Limited]]. During his career at Chicago and Exxon, he had sabbatical appointments at [[University of Cambridge|Cambridge University]] (1957–1958 and 1972–1973), the [[University of Rome Tor Vergata|University of Rome]] (1964–1965), [[Kyoto University]] (1979), the [[University of Amsterdam]] (1991–1992), and the Scottish Universities Physics Alliance (2007).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cohen, Morrel H. |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11503016.html |access-date=2022-09-23 |website=history.aip.org}}</ref>

Cohen retired from Exxon in 1996, serving as Emeritus Senior Scientist until 2000. He then took post-retirement positions in the Physics and Astronomy Department of Rutgers University and the Chemistry and Chemical Biology Department of Princeton University.

== Scientific research and contributions ==
Cohen’s primary research field is theoretical condensed matter physics, with a focus on [[superconductivity]]. Cohen has four patents. Seven of his publications have over 1,000 citations each, according to [[Google Scholar]].

* "Quadrupole Effects in Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Studies of Solids" (M.H. Cohen, F. Reif), Solid State Physics <u>5</u>, 321 (1957). [[doi:10.1016/S0081-1947(08)60105-8]]
* "Self-Consistent Field Approach to the Many Electron Problem" (H. Ehrenreich, M.H. Cohen), Phys. Rev. 115, 786 (1959). [https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRev.115.786 doi:10.1103/PhysRev.115.786] 
* "Molecular Transport in Liquids and Glasses" (M.H. Cohen, D. Turnbull), J. Chem. Phys. 31, 1164 (1959). [[doi:10.1063/1.1730566]]
* "A Free Volume Model of the Amorphous Phase: The Glass Transition" (D. Turnbull, M.H. Cohen), J. Chem. Phys. 34, 120 (1961). [[doi:10.1063/1.1731549]]
* "Simple Band Model for Amorphous Semiconducting Alloys" (M.H. Cohen, H. Fritzsche, S.R. Ovshinsky), Phys. Rev. Letts. 22, 1065 (1969). [[doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.22.1065]]
* "Liquid-Glass Transition, A Free-Volume Approach" (M.H. Cohen, G.S. Grest), Phys. Rev. B 20, 1077 (1979). [[doi:10.1103/PhysRevB.20.1077]]
* "A Self-Similar Model for Sedimentary Rocks with Application to the Dielectric Constant of Fused Glass Beads", (P.N. Sen, C. Scala), Geophysics 46, 781 (1981). [[doi:10.1190/1.1441215]]

In 1962, Cohen, [[Leopoldo Máximo Falicov|Falicov]], and [[James Charles Phillips|Phillips]] calculated the [[Josephson effect|tunneling current]] between normal and superconducting metals across a barrier.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cohen |first1=M. H. |last2=Falicov |first2=L. M. |last3=Phillips |first3=J. C. |date=1962-04-15 |title=Superconductive Tunneling |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.8.316 |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=8 |issue=8 |pages=316–318 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.8.316|bibcode=1962PhRvL...8..316C |url-access=subscription }}</ref> This confirmed a prediction [[Brian Josephson]] had made about the current between two superconducting metals, taking Josephson a step along his path towards his Nobel prize.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Josephson |first=B. D. |date=1974-05-03 |title=The Discovery of Tunneling Supercurrents |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.184.4136.527 |journal=Science |language=en |volume=184 |issue=4136 |pages=527–530 |doi=10.1126/science.184.4136.527 |pmid=17755018 |bibcode=1974Sci...184..527J |issn=0036-8075|url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

Cohen was a mentor to [[Marvin L. Cohen]], who called him "an impressive mentor".<ref>Interview of Marvin Cohen by David Zierler on April 7, 2020, Niels Bohr Library & Archives, American Institute of Physics, College Park, MD USA. [https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/44667]</ref> Cohen was thesis advisor to [[Eleftherios Economou]].

In addition to his research in condensed matter physics, Cohen published research in the application of statistical physics to the fields of [[biology]] and [[econophysics]].

Cohen also contributed to the history of physics, writing memoirs of his interactions with [[Elihu Abrahams]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Cohen, Morrel H. Berkeley days: how great events shaped our careers, for Elihu Abrahams at his 80th birthday celebration, 2007 |url=https://repository.aip.org/node/8155 |access-date=2022-09-23 |website=Niels Bohr Library & Archives |language=en}}</ref> [[Enrico Fermi]],<ref>Cohen, Morrel H. (2004). ''"Remembering Fermi''". In F. Mallamace & H. Eugene Stanley (eds.), The Physics of Complex Systems: New Advances and Perspectives_. Ios Press. pp. 1.</ref> and [[David Turnbull (materials scientist)|David Turnbull]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cohen |first=Morrel H. |date=1985 |title=An Appreciation of Dave Turnbull |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1557/PROC-57-31 |journal=MRS Proceedings |language=en |volume=57 |pages=31 |doi=10.1557/PROC-57-31 |issn=0272-9172|url-access=subscription }}</ref> coauthoring with Marvin L. Cohen an obituary<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cohen |first1=Marvin L. |last2=Cohen |first2=Morrel H. |date=2019-10-01 |title=Charles Kittel |journal=Physics Today |volume=72 |issue=10 |pages=73 |doi=10.1063/PT.3.4326 |bibcode=2019PhT....72j..73C |s2cid=216580309 |issn=0031-9228|doi-access=free }}</ref> for Charles Kittel, and giving an oral history interview<ref>{{Cite web |last=Physics |first=American Institute of |date=2015-01-14 |title=Morrel Cohen |url=https://www.aip.org/history-programs/niels-bohr-library/oral-histories/4559 |access-date=2022-09-23 |website=www.aip.org |language=en}}</ref> to the [[American Institute of Physics]] in 1981.

== Selected honors and appointments ==

* Fellow, [[John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation]] (1957–1958)
* Member, Advisory Panel on Electrophysics, [[National Aeronautics and Space Administration]] (1962–1966)
* Acting Director, [[James Franck Institute]], University of Chicago (1965–1966)
* Director, James Franck Institute, University of Chicago (1968–1971)
* Doctor of Science (honorary), Worcester Polytechnic Institute (1973)
* Director, [[National Science Foundation]] (NSF) Materials Research Laboratory, University of Chicago (1977–1981)
* Member, National Academy of Sciences (1978)
* Fellow, [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (1995)
